summary:
Consensual same-sex intimacy was criminalised in 1961 and decriminalised in 1993, when all references were removed from the criminal code. The age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited across several separate instruments: Section 14.1.1 of the Penal Code, in force since 1 July 2017, bans discrimination on both grounds; Article 1.3.2 of the Criminal Law adopted on 3 December 2015 bars discrimination in criminalisation and sentencing on grounds including sexual and gender orientation; and Article 6 of the Labour Code, since 2022, bans discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. The protections remain fragmented and no comprehensive equality law is in place. A residual offence addressing 'satisfaction of immoral sexual needs' remains on the statute book and can be invoked as a pretext against gender-nonconforming people, although no provision specifically criminalises homosexuality.

Hate-crime provisions: the Criminal Code adopted on 3 December 2015 added sexual orientation and gender identity as protected grounds, scheduled for 1 September 2016 and postponed to 1 July 2017. Section 10(1)(2)(14) aggravates penalties for homicide motivated by hatred of the victim's gender identity or sexual orientation, and hate speech on the basis of gender identity is outlawed. Enforcement does not match the statute: local reports and activists say police continue to disregard or not take seriously complaints of hate crimes against LGBT people, and attacks often result in no punishment.

Legal gender recognition: a June 2009 amendment to Article 20(1) of the Civil Registration Law allows a transgender person to change legal gender on a birth certificate or citizen identification card after sex reassignment surgery. Following the 2019 charging of a police officer for assaulting a detained transgender woman, the police force adopted guidelines requiring officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identity documents.

Partner recognition: Article 16(11) of the Constitution defines marriage as based on the equality and mutual consent of a man and a woman, and no form of union recognition is available. A trans visitor in a relationship the law would class as same-sex has no route to recognition, and such households are ineligible for the protections extended to opposite-sex couples.

Violence and social climate: in September 2009 three transgender women were kidnapped in daylight on a promenade in Ulaanbaatar, driven to a cemetery on the city outskirts, and beaten and sexually assaulted by nine men; the attack was not reported to police for fear of victimisation and reprisal. In February 2014 a gay man was sexually assaulted by a hyper-nationalist group, and in 2001 a lesbian woman was raped, abducted and stabbed by two men. A 2012 National Human Rights Commission survey found almost 80 per cent of LGBT people had experienced human-rights abuse in the previous three years, with almost three-quarters having considered suicide because of intolerance; a 2013 report put the share of LGBT Mongolians who had considered suicide above 73 per cent, and a 2019 report found 79 per cent of LGBT-identified young people had experienced bullying, discrimination or ostracism. Mongolian culture remains strongly heteronormative, and ostracism, harassment and violence persist socially and systemically.

Protection machinery and visibility: LGBT organisations can register. After the 2019 assault case the LGBT Centre trained more than 500 police officers, prosecutors and judges on the 2017 hate-crime provisions, building on earlier training of more than 300 officials as of August 2018. A transgender man who co-founded and advises the LGBT Centre came out in 2004 and began transition in 2011; the 2018 Pride event and the Centre's advocacy are the visible ground for trans life, transition access and acceptance in Ulaanbaatar.
tangentialFactors:
A January 2014 working-group draft would have added hate-bias motive as an aggravating factor, with penalties and reparations for psychological as well as physical damage and police training to recognise and report hate acts. The Justice Ministry replaced it in late May 2014 with generalised discrimination references. As of June 2014 the law provided no additional penalty for bias-motivated violence and no requirement for law enforcement to record a suspected bias motive; the hate-crime grounds that took effect on 1 July 2017 came after that failure.

The commercial and social scene has virtually no presence, venues or activism. A 2008 account describes two organisations holding furtive monthly parties whose attendees feared being outed.

A December 2018 social experiment in Ulaanbaatar placed a gay man, a lesbian and a transgender man roadside to observe public reactions. Responses ranged from death threats and negative comments to positive ones, and the public was more welcoming of the lesbian and the trans man than of the gay man.
localsOnly:
Residents: Article 6 of the Labour Code, in force since 2022, bans employment discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Legal gender recognition on birth certificates and citizen identification cards requires sex reassignment surgery under the 2009 amendment to the Civil Registration Law.

Education and youth: a 2019 report found 79 per cent of LGBT-identified young people had experienced bullying, discrimination or ostracism, and several LGBT students reported discrimination and bullying at school.

Community: LGBT organisations can register, and the LGBT Centre operates in Ulaanbaatar as the principal advocacy body, with a transgender man among its co-founders. Transition access and acceptance are concentrated in the capital.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Asian Development Bank study on the legal status of sexual and gender minorities in Asia and the Pacific carries no finding on Mongolia. No sourced material was identified on entry or visa rules specific to trans travellers, on bathroom or facilities law, or on conversion practices.

The 2012 National Human Rights Commission survey and the 2013 and 2019 reports are dated, and the sources do not set out their methodology or sample sizes. The enforcement picture rests on activist and local reporting rather than official complaint or prosecution data, and no official count of hate-crime complaints or outcomes was identified.

The reasons the Justice Ministry replaced the January 2014 draft in late May 2014 are not documented in the sources.
